opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't think of it that way, at least not in the moment. Of course I knew what I was walking away from. Anyone who has been at a fast-growing AI company knows the equity can be very meaningful, and people around me were quick to point that out. But when I was actually making the decision, money wasn't the main question I was asking myself.

The question was more like: where can I have the most impact over the next several years, and what kind of work do I want to wake up excited about? For me, a lot of that comes back to systems and infrastructure: making large models run efficiently and making that work available to more people, not just a few labs. I felt there was something I wanted to build that I couldn't fully pursue where I was.

And I think in this field, if you optimize too hard for the short-term financial outcome, you can end up making decisions you regret. Things move so fast. The opportunities that matter most often look risky at first. So I tried to trust my judgment about the work itself and assume that if the work is good, the rest tends to follow.

So was it a sacrifice? On paper, maybe. But it didn't feel like giving something up. It felt more like choosing the direction I actually believed in.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I never thought about it as a sacrifice. Of course people around me did the math — unvested equity, the trajectory of a company like xAI — and from the outside it looks like walking away from a lot. But for me, money was never the main variable in that decision.

What I cared about was the kind of work I wanted to do and who I wanted to do it with. I had spent years on open-source systems — SGLang, the serving infrastructure work — and that community mattered a lot to me. At a big lab you work on one piece of a very large machine, and that's valuable, but I wanted to build something where the roadmap was ours, where we could move quickly and the results would be open to everyone.

I'd also say the risk felt different from the inside. When you've been close to the models and the infrastructure, you see how much demand there is for inference, for efficiency, for tooling. So leaving didn't feel like jumping off a cliff. It felt like betting on something I understood well.

And frankly, if things don't work out, I'm still a researcher and an engineer. The skills don't disappear. That makes it much easier to take the leap than people assume.

For me, the question was which path I wanted to spend the next few years on, rather than which one might have the highest financial upside.
